title: Two Interpretations : An Explanation
paragraphs: Kōvalan the son of Mācāttuvān And Kaṇṇaki the daughter of Māṇāykaṉ Were united in wedlock On the auspicious hour of the auspicious day, The vedic rites being prescribed by the ripe brahmin priest And the bridal couple circumambulating the sacrificial fire.

The auspicious time and day prescribed Did not guard against the separation of Kōvalan From the virtuous Kaṇṇaki, The woman on whom Kōvalan on the nuptial bed showered praises like ‘Gold with no blemish’ ‘Pearl with right-turned curls’ ‘Fragrance unadulterated’ ‘Sugar cane’ and ‘honey’; Nor did they protect the nuptial cord of Kaṇṇaki. They but pierced through his wedded life like swords and spears.
Kaṇṇaki lost her husband and became a widow. The king hurled at her the charge of being a thief’s wife.

The vedic mantras recited by the brahmin priest And the propitious time of wedding fixed on the planetary motion Didn’t protect the conjugal harmony of the couple. The epic Cilappatikāram is witness to this fact.
The matchless Tolkāppiyam, That is the treasure trove of the Tamils And a fine flower-garden of language and literature, Preceded Cilappatikāram by a long span of time.
The culture of the Tamils Didn’t see complete degeneration In the early days of the Aryan advent.
The inroads of the alien influence nevertheless Were marked here and there. Why should it be denied? Tolkāppiyar himself makes pointed references to it.

In the clandestine love career, That precedes the wedded life of the lovers, The hero does not eschew rendezvous with the heroine On account of the inhospitable path of the wilderness, The intense vigil of the heroine’s kin, The perils due to the wild animals, Or the thought of the long travel to make.
And yet Commentator Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar presumes that The rendezvous used to be deferred For reasons of time and day inauspicious (ōrai).
Another commentator Iḷampūraṇar too Almost concurs in this regard with the former.
On the other hand, Veḷḷaivāraṇar’s Tolkāppiyam study Looks at the word ōrai

As meaning sport and festivities. He says The hero takes part in the sports of the town In the company of his close companions, That would act as a cover Protecting him from the scandal of the villagefolk About his visit to the heroine’s place.
And Veḷḷaivāraṇar provides us several instances, Not just one or two, Where ōrai refers to play and festivities.
Going by which We can establish that Tolkāppiyar uses the term ōrai In the sense of play And not auspicious hour.

Where we insist that Veḷḷaivāraṇar is unacceptable And that ōrai is observing propitious hour, It might then mean that Beliefs in day and time auspicious Are an intrusion into the Tamil life As is the visitation of snakes and scorpions.

> During the clandestine career > The hero does not go by > Signs of the zodiac and auspicious day > For his rendezvous with the heroine. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 44) > > Deterred the hero is not too > From his rendezvous with the heroine > By the hardness of the path, > The dispiritedness (born of hostile men and things around), > And by the fear of perils and obstacles to his love. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 45)
